results.summary_before: This design converts an 8-bit binary number to a decimal number displayed as three BCD digits on a 7-segment display, using the Double Dabble algorithm. The conversion is implemented with combinational logic, while a state machine sequentially displays hundreds, tens, ones, and a decimal point. The design has an 8-bit binary input, an 8-bit output for the 7-segment display, and an 8-bit bidirectional port that outputs the tens and ones. It requires no external hardware and has been tested with several binary values.

results.summary_before: This project implements an all-digital phase-locked loop (ADPLL) with a phase-frequency detector, proportional-integral loop filter, 24-bit phase-accumulator digitally controlled oscillator, and a leaky-bucket lock detector. It uses a reference input on ui_in[0] and outputs the DCO clock and lock status on uo_out[1] and uo_out[0] respectively. Testing involves providing a system clock and a reference square wave, then monitoring the outputs with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to verify frequency tracking and lock assertion. The design is notable for its fully digital architecture and configurable lock thresholds.

results.summary_before: This design multiplies two 2x2 matrices of signed 8-bit elements into signed 16-bit results using a systolic array of four multiply-add-accumulate processing elements. It is controlled through eight data inputs plus load, transpose, activation, and done signals, with results presented on eight output pins, and it is intended to be driven by an external microcontroller that supplies the clock and coordinates I/O. It stores two input matrices in registers and includes a control unit and feeder module to schedule data through the array. The documentation claims over 99.8 million operations per second in a streamed processing pattern, though no silicon measurements are reported.

results.summary_before: This project implements an analog-controlled 8-pin multiplexer that selects among eight test circuits based on an input voltage from 0V to 1.8V, with thresholds every 200mV. The test circuits include various ring oscillators (3, 5, 7 inverters), frequency dividers using T flip-flops, and a resistor divider, allowing comprehensive testing of the design. The multiplexer uses only two analog pins: one for control voltage and one for the selected output. Testing requires a laboratory power supply, multimeter, and oscilloscope to measure frequencies and signal characteristics.

results.summary_before: This project is an instantiation of the SumItUp hardware thread from Don Thomas's textbook and CMU's 18-341 course, which accumulates a series of 8-bit values presented on the input pins. When go_l is asserted the thread begins adding subsequent values until the input equals zero, at which point done is asserted and the 8-bit sum appears on the outputs, with carry beyond eight bits discarded. No external hardware is required, and the author plans to write cocotb testbenches for verification. The design is a simple educational example of a hardware thread with a handshake interface.
